title: Aryna Sabalenka’s rankings drop confirmed as her WTA Finals prize money & points are revealed
article_text:
Aryna Sabalenka’s 2026 season has been far from satisfying and she tasted further disappointment with an early exit from the WTA Finals on Friday.

Despite never lifting the title at the WTA Finals, Sabalenka had reached at least the semi-final of the tournament in the past four years, with her only previous round-robin exit coming in her event debut back in 2021.

However, the 28-year-old was unable to secure her spot in the semi-final this year in Indian Wells, falling in three sets to Elina Svitolina in a crucial encounter.

Sabalenka’s campaign started with an opening win against Karolina Muchova on Monday, though she slumped to a heavy 6-4, 6-0 defeat to Mirra Andreeva in her second match.

With Svitolina losing to Andreeva but then defeating Muchova, both she and Sabalenka knew their clash on Friday was a winner-takes-all contest.

Sabalenka had won six of her seven previous meetings against Svitolina but was unable to produce her best tennis, and it was her Ukrainian opponent who claimed an impressive 6-3, 3-6, 6-1 triumph.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Svitolina will now face Linda Noskova in the last four, but Sabalenka finds herself out of the tournament — and slipping down the WTA Rankings.

No ranking points were awarded to any of the eight finalists for qualifying for the tournament, meaning they all started on a clean slate heading into the event.

Each round-robin match win was worth 200 ranking points, with no points on offer for losing at this stage of the tournament.

With one win and two defeats in Indian Wells, Sabalenka takes home 200 ranking points from Indian Wells, meaning she will end the season on 6,685 points.

That is a notable decrease on the 10,870 points she ended 2025 with and, having already lost her world No 1 ranking to Elena Rybakina in September, she will now drop further in the WTA Rankings.

Andreeva’s win over Sabalenka in the round-robin stage saw the Russian move above the Belarusian in the WTA Live Rankings, and she is now guaranteed to be ranked above Sabalenka next Monday regardless of how the she fares across the rest of her campaign.

Sabalenka is provisionally down to world No 3 in the WTA Live Rankings, though she would fall further to world No 4 if Jessica Pegula wins the title in Indian Wells.

A total of 400 ranking points are on offer for the two women who prevail in Saturday’s semi-finals, with a further 500 points on offer in Sunday’s final.

By qualifying for the WTA Finals, Sabalenka and her fellow participants in the singles draw secured a participation fee of $220,000 ahead of action.

Each round-robin match win was then worth a further $230,000, with a total of $690,000 on offer for an unbeaten round-robin record; in Indian Wells, only Andreeva was able to achieve this.

With one win and two defeats to her name in Indian Wells, Sabalenka will take home a total prize money payout of $450,000 from the WTA Finals in 2026.

title: How a pro incredibly won his DP World Tour card — after ‘standstill traffic’
article_text:
Tom Lewis can tell you all that’s happened to him over the past couple of weeks at DP World Tour Qualifying School.

It’s just that the 35-year-old Englishman thinks because it’s so unreal, the words may fall short.

“Yeah, I mean, these things happen,” Lewis said, “you can’t write it.”

– The exit. Across a 15-year pro career, Lewis has seen some success. A pair of DP World Tour wins. A Korn Ferry Tour win. He’d also played on a Walker Cup team, and he was the low amateur at the 2011 Open Championship. But this year, he played mostly on the Hotel Planner Tour, the circuit below the DP World Tour, and finished 89th in the season-long points race. He entered Q-School. Maybe he’d make a run. But at the second stage event at Fontanals Golf Club in Spain, he finished 23rd, and only the top 21 and ties moved on to the final stage tournament.

– The traffic. According to the DP World Tour, Lewis got stuck in “standstill traffic,” and the Irish Golfer reported that that caused him to miss a flight. But there was a silver lining, albeit a small one. A playoff to determine final-stage alternates was bumped back to Nov. 2, and Lewis could now play in it.

– The return. He didn’t just play in it; Lewis told the DP World Tour that he played the hole “like a video game,” and he became the eighth alternate. Still, his chances of moving on remained low.

Then Lewis was in. He told the DP World Tour that while he was boarding his flight back home to England, he learned that he made the final stage event, which started last Friday and ended Wednesday at Infinitum Golf course, also in Spain.

“My manager is caddying for me this week,” Lewis told the DP World Tour, “and he said that he thinks it’s probably the weirdest two hours we’ve ever had together and we’ve worked together for 10 years.”

– The comeback. At the grueling, six-round, final stage tourney, Lewis shined. He shot rounds of 67, 68, 65, 67, 63 and 68, and he finished fifth — giving him a DP World Tour card for the first time since the 2024 season.

Afterward, the DP World Tour asked him if he had a message for those who follow him.

“I’m really pleased for them to prove them right, really, because I usually suck,” he said. “This time, it’s nice to give them something to cheer about. So my phone’s obviously going off in my pocket right now.

“So there’s a lot of people to congratulate me, and I’m going to get back to them tonight. And yeah, it’s going to be good to get home and spend the time with my wife and celebrate with them.”

Thursday, Lewis also posted to Instagram.

He had some words for all that had happened.

“I just want to say how close things are and how quickly it changes. Fate? Maybe.

“Nov. 2: I’m one shot away from genuinely getting a job and walking away from golf and into the shadows. One playoff, one hole, one birdie, eighth alternate for the finals.

“Nov. 11: 108 holes later, with seven missed greens and only four bogeys all week and 30-under, I’m back with the big boys. I’ve missed them!

“2027 is going to bring ups and downs, but I’m ready for the challenge. I’m coming for you with everything I have.”

title: Austin Championship merchandise gets Texas makeover after Good Good sponsorship fallout
article_text:
For Phillips, who oversees all tour operations for Levelwear — managing everything from merchandise stands to volunteer uniforms — the Austin event offered a rare break from the standard tour routine. Over the last eight to 10 years, golf tournament retail had grown somewhat standardized across stops, often relying on massive, uniform buys. Starting from scratch with a new logo in a city like Austin meant throwing out the usual playbook.

"Once I got the logo, it was a lot of fun to have the creativity and the freedom to create whatever I wanted," Phillips said of the rapid turnaround. "It was a lot in a couple weeks because everything had to get produced so quickly ... It was a lot of fun that I normally don't get to do on the normal tour stuff."

To make the tent at Barton Creek Resort's Fazio Canyons course feel distinctly local rather than off-the-rack, Phillips leaned heavily into Texas culture and Austin's iconic creative identity. As a Houston native, he had an intuitive sense of what might resonate with the crowd. He designed T-shirts and headwear featuring nods to the city's bat bridge, local beverage culture and classic Lone Star State motifs.

He also drew directly from Austin's deep musical and cinematic roots, blending a "Dazed and Confused" aesthetic with Willie Nelson-inspired designs. Once the concepts were approved by tournament organizers, the sprint to production began to get the racks stocked in time for opening day.

By the time the gates opened, that local-first approach was already paying off. While fans browsed a wide mix of apparel rather than gravitating toward a single item, pieces with unmistakable Austin and Texas flair clearly led the pack.

"It's been interesting here because it's been a little bit of everything," Phillips noted, looking out over the bustling tent. "It's not like one style's flying out of here. But anything that is more locally themed is moving faster for sure."

title: Mateo Sanguinetti Becomes Second Uruguayan Test Centurion and First Americas Prop to Reach 100 Caps
article_text:
When Mateo Sanguinetti runs onto the pitch at Trailfinders Sports Ground in London this Saturday to face Zimbabwe, the 34-year-old loose head prop will etch his name permanently into rugby history. Earning his 100th Test cap for Los Teros, Sanguinetti becomes just the second Uruguayan player, following former teammate Diego Magno, to reach the century mark, and the first prop from anywhere in the Americas to achieve the milestone.

Sanguinetti’s journey to 100 caps began in Montevideo at his beloved home club, Los Cuervos, where he started playing at age 10. After rising through Uruguay’s age-grade ranks, he made his senior Test debut against Paraguay in Asunción in April 2014. At the time, Uruguay was an amateur outfit battling to return to the global stage after missing consecutive tournaments. Sanguinetti immediately became part of the historic 2014 repechage qualifying campaign against Russia, culminating in the unforgettable victory in Montevideo that punched Uruguay’s ticket to Rugby World Cup 2015 in England and Wales.

That triumph sparked the modern rebirth of Uruguayan rugby, and Sanguinetti has been a constant pillar through every step of the transformation from amateurism to full-time professionalism. Following the 2015 tournament, he took his talents abroad to help spearhead Uruguay’s professional wave. In 2019, he moved to the USA to play in Major League Rugby with the Houston SaberCats alongside Diego Magno. He subsequently returned home to join Peñarol for the launch of South America’s professional club league before spending two seasons in France with RC Massy (2020–2022), helping the French club earn promotion to the Pro D2. Since 2022, he has remained a cornerstone of Peñarol’s dominant front row in Super Rugby Americas.

On the international stage, Sanguinetti’s durability is unmatched among front-rowers. Across three Rugby World Cup campaigns—England 2015, Japan 2019, and France 2023—he has accumulated 11 Rugby World Cup caps (starting nine of those matches), placing him alongside the all-time Uruguayan leaders for World Cup appearances. His tournament highlights include Uruguay’s famous 2019 upset victory over Fiji in Kamaishi and competitive battles against tier-one giants like France, Italy, and the All Blacks in 2023.

With his 100th cap secured against Zimbabwe, an all-time Uruguayan record is suddenly within sight. Sanguinetti sits just seven appearances behind Diego Magno’s national record of 107 Test caps. Given his form, fitness, and central role under head coach Guzmán Barreiro, surpassing Magno and leading Los Teros into a fourth consecutive tournament at Rugby World Cup 2027 in Australia is well within his reach.

It may be along time before Sanguinetti and Magno are joined by more Uruguayan centurions. Veteran second-rower Ignacio Dotti (76 caps) and hooker Germán Kessler (75 caps) are well-positioned if they continue beyond Rugby World Cup 2027.

title: Springboks show true colours after France loss as Rassie Erasmus says it's over
article_text:
Rassie Erasmus admitted South Africa's Nations Championship dream is effectively over after their dramatic 21-19 defeat to France – and refused to make excuses for his side's performance.

The Springboks head coach refused to criticise a series of disciplinary decisions, including a 20-minute red card for Jasper Wiese and two other yellow cards, as his side suffered their first defeat of the competition in Paris on Friday night.

But a dignified Erasmus said there were no excuses, instead admitting his players had not performed well enough and that their lack of discipline had cost them dearly.

"We didn't play well, so don’t find a lot of excuses," he said. "I don't think there's much more to blame than ourselves."

He was equally frank about the damage the result had done to South Africa's hopes of lifting the inaugural Nations Championship trophy.

"I think we basically killed our dreams for the Nations Championship tonight with this performance and not getting the win and the four tries," he said.

It was a candid assessment from Erasmus after a night which had already seen him attract attention for all the wrong reasons before kick-off, having once again made wholesale changes to his starting front row just an hour before the match.

Erasmus switched all three front-row positions shortly before the game, promoting Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit into the starting XV and moving Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw to the replacements bench.

The Springboks had initially named Nche, Marx and Louw as their starting combination, but the late switch mirrored a tactic Erasmus had employed during the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series against New Zealand.

On that occasion, the South Africa coach explained the decision had been influenced by the weather forecast, with the Springboks believing a different front-row combination would be better suited to the conditions.

However, questions have since been raised over whether such changes are permitted in official international competitions, with some supporters and pundits accusing Erasmus of going against the spirit of the game and calling for World Rugby to clarify its regulations.

World Rugby Regulation 15.1.2 states that participating unions must announce and exchange their starting XV and up to eight replacements 48 hours before kick-off in an international match.

There remains uncertainty over whether named replacements can be promoted into the starting team so close to kick-off, with World Rugby having the power to impose fines for breaches of its regulations and agreements with unions.

Erasmus's decision to repeat the tactic in the Nations Championship has prompted fresh calls for the governing body to make clear exactly what is permitted.

On the pitch, France produced a stunning first-half performance to put themselves in control of the contest.

Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Theo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey all crossed for converted tries to give Les Bleus a commanding 21-7 half-time lead, with Wessels scoring South Africa's only try of the opening period.

South Africa's task became even more difficult early in the second half when Wiese was shown a yellow card for a dangerous tackle, which was upgraded to a 20-minute red card following a bunker review.

Lood de Jager had also been yellow-carded for a high tackle, with South Africa conceding 11 penalties during the match, eight of them in their own half.

But despite being down to 14 men, the Springboks produced an impressive fightback, with Cobus Reinach touching down after 50 minutes to reduce the deficit to seven points.

France were forced to withstand wave after wave of pressure, with the hosts also losing players to the sin-bin as the contest became increasingly frantic.

When replacement prop Regis Montagne was sent off for 10 minutes with the game entering its final stages, South Africa looked to have broken the home side's resistance.

Back up to 15 players, the visitors made their numerical advantage count when replacement hooker Marx went over from a driving maul.

However, while Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu had converted South Africa's first two tries, replacement fly-half Manie Libbok failed to add the extras, leaving France clinging to a two-point advantage.

The Springboks continued to pile forward in the closing stages, but France held firm to secure a famous victory.

It was their first win over South Africa at the Stade de France since 2005, despite the Springboks having won nine of the previous 10 meetings between the sides, including their dramatic 29-28 victory in the 2023 Rugby World Cup quarter-final.

The result has also had significant implications for the Nations Championship standings.

France took control of the Northern Hemisphere table on 21 points, strengthening their position ahead of their final group fixture against Argentina next week.

South Africa remain top of the Southern Hemisphere standings, also on 21 points, but their position is now under serious threat from New Zealand, who are just one point behind with a game in hand.

The All Blacks face Wales in Cardiff on Saturday before taking on England the following weekend, meaning they could move ahead of the Springboks with victory.

South Africa, meanwhile, travel to Ireland next week for their final group match, with Erasmus admitting the prospect of lifting the first Nations Championship trophy has taken a major hit.

title: Maro Itoje warns England not to sleepwalk into clash with Eddie Jones’s Japan
article_text:
Maro Itoje has insisted England will be ready for any curveballs Eddie Jones may throw on Saturday, warning his side they cannot “sleepwalk” into battle against Japan.

Jones, England’s longest-serving head coach after his stint between 2015 and 2022, has strongly hinted he will set his side up to unsettle his former charges at Twickenham, warning that they do not like “unorthodox” rugby. The hosts are heavy favourites to back up last week’s record win over Australia with another emphatic victory and have never lost to Japan but Steve Borthwick has made 10 personnel and two positional changes, fielding an inexperienced side against that of his predecessor.

“The overarching message this week is that we need to be alive,” said Itoje. “It’s impossible to tick off every eventuality that an opposition might do, especially a team like Japan, who have a very distinct way of playing. They’re very consistent at getting speed into the game. They could do a number of things, so let’s be alive and let’s not sleepwalk into things and think ‘most teams play like this’ because Japan aren’t most teams.

“One, we need to be alive. Two, we need to impose our game. We need to play the way we want to play. Whether it’s unorthodox shapes in attack, things around the set piece. I know they’re going to want to keep the ball in play or come up with special unique plays. If we’re alive and we’ve got our house in order then we should be able to deal with what they throw at us.”

Jones gave Itoje his debut in 2016 and oversaw his development into one of the world’s leading second-rows. When the Australian was in charge, England won three Six Nations titles, including one grand slam, and reached the final of the 2019 World Cup in Japan.

“I’m sure [the crowd] will receive him warmly,” added Itoje. “It’s not the first time he’s been back. Most coaches want to keep you thinking. Eddie would throw a whole load of weird and wonderful things at us to keep us sharp and keep us on our toes.”

Borthwick, meanwhile, has a debt of gratitude to Jones, who gave him his coaching break with Japan before appointing him England assistant. “What [Eddie] does really well is maximises the strengths of any team he coaches,” said Borthwick. “So from coaching the Japan team to coaching the England team, two very different teams, both of which he did really well with.

“One of the aspects that I see is how alive you need to be mentally, emotionally in a game of Test match rugby and the intensity that demands. And I use that word very deliberately with them – you’ve got to be alive. Because what happens is the quality of player you’re playing against, any mental switch-off is the moment where one of these players will find it and go.”

title: Adam Jones named Harlequins head coach for two games
article_text:

title: Bryson DeChambeau announces 'mega' plans to design course for new residential community in his California hometown
article_text:
Oddly, Bryson DeChambeau’s California hometown of Clovis, 10 miles east of Fresno, doesn’t have a golf course. It will have one and a much larger population if the two-time U.S. Open champion and his development partners have their way on what DeChambeau has called a “mega” project.

DeChambeau has announced that he and real estate developer Cook Land Company have plans to build an 18-hole championship course, The Orchard Golf Club, that would be the golfer’s first design, and a residential community on the land they’ve acquired at historic McFarlane Ranch, which has existed for three generations while growing crops such as citrus and almonds.

“The Central Valley has always been a community built on hard work, character, and discipline. Having grown up here and attended Clovis East High School, I feel a deep responsibility to give back to the region that provided me with so much,” DeChambeau said in a statement.

“This is a profound opportunity for my team and I to work with the Cook family to help revitalize the area by investing in a project that uses golf to truly serve the community.”

In a nod to the Central Valley’s primary industry of farming, every hole on the course will be surrounded by a different variety of fruit or nut tree. Clovis is a city of about 120,000, and DeChambeau said on a podcast interview with Joe Pompliano that the development is so large that it could bring up to 30 percent more residents to the city.

DeChambeau noted in his statement on Friday that plans for the development have been discussed since 2022 and that the project still needs approval from the City of Clovis and Fresno County. He estimated that the process could take about 18 months. “The development regulations in California are complex but the City of Clovis and Fresno County has been and will continue to work hand in hand to bring this important project to the region,” he said.

In his statement, DeChambeau did not name an architect who would potentially work with him on the course design elements.

title: 'There's no guarantees': Dave Rennie on overlooked All Blacks trio
article_text:
With Chay Fihaki, Josh Jacomb, and Saula Ma’u waiting in the wings for their chance on the All Blacks‘ Nations Championship Northern Tour, head coach Dave Rennie explained the challenge facing the trio as they wait for an opportunity in the remaining two Tests of 2026.

Many believed the Nations Championship contest against Wales was a chance to give Josh Jacomb a first Test start, while Fihaki and Ma’u remain as depth options heading into the final two weeks of the four-Test tour.

Jacomb started for the All Blacks in their Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry midweek match against the Bulls in Pretoria, and featured off the bench against both the Lions and the Sharks.

The new Highlanders recruit currently sits behind Ruben Love, Damian McKenzie, and Richie Mo’unga in the pecking order, while experienced veteran Beauden Barrett is also an option in the No.10 jersey.

For Ma’u, he had one appearance off the bench in the All Blacks’ 41-35 victory over the Lions in Johannesburg, but is stuck behind both Fletcher Newell and Pasilio Tosi on the end-of-year tour.

Fihaki, who made his Test debut off the bench at Sydney’s Accor Stadium in the 2026 Bledisloe Cup Test match against Australia, could come into the selection picture against England with Will Jordan nursing a hamstring tear, but seems unlikely.

When asked about why the trio didn’t feature in the 23-man squad for the Wales Test match in Cardiff, Rennie outlined his reasoning.

“There are no guarantees. We talk a lot about earning the right to play, and all three of the guys who missed out in selection in the first two weeks have all played in the jersey before,” Rennie said in Cardiff.

“Obviously, Chay got a Test debut in Sydney, and the other two boys played in Africa. So, doesn’t mean that they won’t get an opportunity on this tour. But yeah, based on, you know, obviously Richie coming back, that made sense.

“Some, you know, we were keen to have, obviously, Beauden in the mix as well, and he can cover 10 so look, certainly the three boys who haven’t stripped yet are determined, and their jobs to continue to train well and apply pressure.

“We just decided in the end it will give us a little bit more experience. I mean, if we got under pressure with so many guys lacking experience, it could put us under a bit of pressure.

“We want to pay respect to Wales too. We‘ve picked a side that we think will show some respect for them.”

Rennie provided an update on the fitness of Jordan, who is touch and go for the Nations Championship finals weekend after picking up a minor “hamstring tear” against Scotland.

“Yeah, no, he’s a chance to be available in the last week,” the All Blacks coach said.

“He’s got boxes to tick along the way, so he’s been doing a little bit of strength work over the last couple of days, and the plan is to run him Saturday, I think.

“And if he has any setbacks amongst that, then he’s likely to return home. But at this stage, he’s a chance to play in that final week, so he’ll remain in camp.”

title: NNL: Sunshine Stars land sponsorship deal
Two Malaysian pairs reach Kaohsiung Masters finals
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will have two chances to win titles at the Kaohsiung Masters after both Ong Xin Yee-Carmen Ting and Wee Yee Hern-Vannee Gobi reached their respective finals on Saturday.

Women's pair Xin Yee-Carmen will face familiar opponents in their bid for a first World Tour title, while mixed doubles combination Yee Hern-Vannee will face an Olympic silver medallist.

World No. 26 Xin Yee-Carmen eased past Taiwan's Lin Yen Yu-Wang Yi Zhen 21-13, 21-9 in the semi-final of the Super 100 tournament at the Kaohsiung Arena.

"Xin Yee and Carmen's emotional control, preparation and execution of the game plan were good, and they did well in carrying out what we had planned," said coach Wong Pei Tty.

"Tomorrow's final will be a tough challenge against opponents they have known since they were young.

"The main thing is to stay composed and execute our game plan throughout the match."

Top seeds Xin Yee-Carmen will meet Indonesia's world No. 31 Isyana Syahira Meida-Rinjani Kwinnara Nastine in Sunday's final, a rematch of last year's Guwahati Masters title decider. Meida-Nastine won 21-17, 23-21 in Guwahati and also beat Xin Yee-Carmen 16-21, 21-14, 21-14 in the first round of the Thailand Open in May.

The Indonesians lead their head-to-head record 5-2, including matches at junior level.

Xin Yee-Carmen have twice finished runners-up on the World Tour, having lost to Bulgaria's Gabriela Stoeva-Stefani Stoeva in the Odisha Masters final last December.

Earlier, world No. 83 Yee Hern-Vannee reached their first World Tour final together after overcoming Taiwan's world No. 137 Lin Sheng Ming-Sun Liang Ching 21-11, 11-21, 21-8.

The Malaysian fourth seeds also avenged compatriots Wong Tien Ci-Lim Chiew Sien, who were beaten by Sheng Ming-Liang Ching earlier in the tournament.

Yee Hern-Vannee will face South Korea's Ki Dong Ju-Jeong Na Eun for the title after the Koreans defeated Indonesia's Jafar Hidayatullah-Rinjani 21-16, 18-21, 21-17.

Na Eun won the mixed doubles silver medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics with Kim Won Ho, losing to China's Zheng Si Wei-Huang Ya Qiong in the final. Won Ho now forms the world No. 1 men's doubles pair with Seo Seung Jae.
